title: WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgames!
subtitle: A game in a few seconds
summary: WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgames! is a Game Boy Advance collection built from extremely short games. A command appears, the player has only moments to understand it, and the next task follows almost immediately. Wario and his friends organise these microgames into distinct stages, ranging across everyday oddities, sport and Nintendo references. Released in Europe as Minigame Mania, it turns rapid interpretation into the main skill. Learning a complicated control scheme matters less than recognising what this particular few seconds require from a familiar button or direction.
body: WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgames! is a Game Boy Advance collection built from extremely short games. A command appears, the player has only moments to understand it, and the next task follows almost immediately. Wario and his friends organise these microgames into distinct stages, ranging across everyday oddities, sport and Nintendo references. Released in Europe as Minigame Mania, it turns rapid interpretation into the main skill. Learning a complicated control scheme matters less than recognising what this particular few seconds require from a familiar button or direction.

Each new screen asks the player to read an unfamiliar scene quickly. A small mistake costs a life, while successful play drives the sequence onward and increases its pace. Longer boss games interrupt that rhythm and provide a different kind of test. The variety depends on clarity: an image and a short instruction must suggest an action almost at once. WarioWare makes that act of recognition enjoyable in itself, finding comedy in how abruptly one miniature situation can replace another without time for a conventional introduction.

The characters give their stages a flavour rather than merely dividing a menu. 9-Volt’s Nintendo-themed selection, for example, turns familiar gaming imagery into material for the same short format. Unlockable diversions such as Pyoro and Paper Plane show that the collection also has room for games that can be pursued for longer scores. Its origins connect with the Sound Bomber mode of Mario Artist: Polygon Studio. WarioWare develops that rapid-fire idea into a complete identity, with the changes of subject becoming the attraction that holds the collection together.
